text: Motion with constant acceleration. Before using the constant acceleration equations, we need to decide whether this model applies. These equations are powerful, but they only describe motion where the acceleration is constant over the interval being analyzed. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. A car accelerates from rest, then later breaks to a stop. Should the entire trip be modeled with one constant acceleration, or should it be split into separate intervals? Choosing a one-dimensional motion model. Use the following questions before choosing an equation. Is the motion along one straight axis? If yes, the motion can be described with one-dimensional position, velocity, and acceleration. Is the acceleration constant over the interval? If yes, the constant acceleration equations can be used. If no, use graphs, calculus, or split the motion into intervals where the acceleration is approximately constant. Are the known and unknown quantities among x, x0, v, v0, a and t? If yes, choose an equation that contains the unknown and the given quantities. Does the sign of the answer make physical sense? Check whether the object is moving in the expected direction, speeding up or slowing down appropriately, and whether any time value is physically meaningful. A Khan Academy video is linked on the course webpage. Notation. To make things simpler, we introduce some conventions in notation. One simplification is taking t0 equals 0, which is the point in time when you begin to measure. Time exists before this point, but until you get your delorean to 88 miles per hour, then it doesn't make sense to include the past. The elapsed time goes from delta t equals t final minus t0 to delta t equals t final. We don't need the subscript f anymore. So the elapsed time is delta t equals t. We can drop the subscript f from the delta x and delta v as well. In our simplified notation, we have delta t equals t, delta x equals x minus x0, delta v equals v minus v0, where the subscript o denotes an initial value and the absence of a subscript indicates the final value of the variable. For now, we will also make the assumption that the acceleration is constant. As a result, the average and instantaneous acceleration are equal, or average acceleration equals a equals constant. In many situations in this course, the acceleration is constant. When it isn't, for example, a car accelerating to top speed, then breaking to a stop, the motion will be considered in separate parts, like with the runner, and each part has its own constant acceleration. Displacement and position from velocity. To get our first two equations, we start with the definition of average velocity. Average velocity equals delta x over delta t and substitute the simplified notation to get average velocity equals x minus x0 over t. Solving for x gives x equals x0 plus average velocity times t, where the arithmetic average velocity is average velocity equals the quantity v0 plus v divided by 2. This version of average velocity reflects that when acceleration is constant, then average velocity is the simple average of the initial and final velocities, solving for final velocity from acceleration and time. We can derive another useful equation by manipulating the definition of acceleration, a equals delta v over delta t. By substituting the simplified notation for delta v and delta t, we have a equals the quantity v minus v0 divided by t for constant acceleration. Solving for v yields v equals v0 plus a t for constant acceleration. The above equation gives us insight into relationships among velocity, acceleration and time. We can see that final velocity depends on both acceleration and time. For zero acceleration, then the initial and final velocities are equal, that is, v equals v0. If a is less than zero, then v is less than v0. These relationships fit our intuition, which can be a good sign. Example problem, calculating final velocity. The problem, an airplane lands with an initial velocity of 70.0 meters per second and then accelerates opposite to the motion at 1.50 meters per second squared for 40.0 seconds. What is its final velocity? The model. The airplane moves in one dimension with constant acceleration. We choose the initial direction of motion as positive. Since the acceleration is opposite the motion, the acceleration is negative in this coordinate system. The math. For constant acceleration, the final velocity is related to the initial velocity, acceleration, and elapsed time by v equals v0 plus at. The acceleration is negative because it points opposite the positive direction of motion. So the velocity time relation gives v equals v0 plus at equals 70.0 meters per second plus the quantity negative 1.50 meters per second squared times 40.0 seconds equals 10.0 meters per second. The conclusion. The airplane's final velocity is 10.0 meters per second. The result is still positive, so the airplane is still moving in its original direction after 40.0 seconds but it has slowed substantially. Solving for final position with constant acceleration. We can use the equation that defines the average velocity, which is related to time and displacement with the arithmetic definition of average velocity. This gives us three equations. x equals x0 plus average velocity times t. Average velocity equals 1.50 times the quantity v plus v0, and v equals v0 plus at. Where a is a constant acceleration and we are using our simplified notation. The third equation can be substituted into the second equation to get average velocity equals 1.50 times the quantity 2.0 plus at, which equals v0 plus 1.50 at. Now we substitute this expression for the average velocity into the equation for displacement, yielding x equals x0 plus average velocity times t, which equals x0 plus v0 times t plus 1.50 at squared. The position equation can also be written using the final velocity instead of the initial velocity. This form is useful when v, a, and t are known, but v0 is not needed. The velocity equation can be solved for the initial velocity, which gives v equals v0 plus at. So v0 equals v minus at. The position equation can then be rewritten by replacing v0 with v minus at, which gives x equals x0 plus v0 times t plus 1.50 at squared, which equals x0 plus the quantity v minus at times t plus 1.50 at squared. Expanding and combining the acceleration terms gives the equivalent position equation x equals x0 plus vt minus at squared plus 1.50 at squared, which equals x0 plus vt minus 1.50 at squared. Writing this result in displacement form gives x minus x0 equals vt minus 1.50 at squared. This equation describes the same constant acceleration motion, but it is written in terms of the final velocity v rather than the initial velocity v0. We can see the following relationships from the above equation. Displacement depends on time squared when the acceleration is not zero. The form of the equation is a quadratic, so it should plot as a parabola. If the acceleration is zero, then it reduces to x equals x0 plus v0 times t, the equation for displacement under constant velocity v0. Example problem. Calculating displacement of an accelerating object. The problem. Dragsters can achieve an average acceleration of 26.0 meters per second squared. Suppose a dragster accelerates from rest at this rate for 5.56 seconds. How far does it travel in this time? The model. The dragster is modeled as a particle moving in one dimension with constant acceleration. It starts from rest at the starting line, which we choose as the origin. With these choices, the displacement is determined by the acceleration and the elapsed time. The math. For one-dimensional motion with constant acceleration, the position is given by x equals x0 plus v0 times t plus 1 half a t squared. Because the dragster starts from rest at the origin, v0 equals 0 and x0 equals 0, so the position equation reduces to x equals 1 half a t squared. The displacement after 5.56 seconds is found by evaluating this expression, which gives x equals 1 half times 26.0 meters per second squared times the quantity 5.56 seconds squared equals 402 meters. The conclusion. The dragster travels 402 meters while accelerating from rest for 5.56 seconds. The large displacement over a short time is physically reasonable because the acceleration is very large. Solving for final velocity from distance and acceleration. Since the acceleration a is constant, we can solve for the time t and substitute it into the equation for displacement. We have the following equations. t equals the quantity v minus v0 divided by a. Average velocity equals 1 half times the quantity v plus v0 and x equals x0 plus average velocity times t. Substituting the first and second equations into the final equation and performing some algebra gives x equals x0 plus 1 half times the quantity v plus v0 times the quantity v minus v0 divided by a. Which equals x0 plus 1 half a times the quantity v minus v0 times the quantity v plus v0. Which equals x0 plus 1 half a times the quantity v squared minus v0 squared. This is a one-dimensional pursuit problem involving two objects. We choose the point where the gazelle passes the cheetah as the origin and take the direction of motion as positive. The cheetah starts from rest with constant acceleration so its position is X sub C equals 1 half A sub C T squared. Part A. At the catch time the two positions are equal, which gives X sub G equals X sub C. V sub G T equals 1 half A sub C T squared. The non-zero catch time is found by dividing both sides by T and solving for T, which gives V sub G equals 1 half A sub C T. T equals 2 V sub G over A sub C equals 2 times 10 meters per second divided by 4.0 meters per second squared equals 5.0 seconds. Part B. The catch displacement is found by evaluating the gazelle's position at T equals 5.0 seconds, which gives X sub G equals V sub G T. Equals 10 meters per second times 5.0 seconds equals 50 meters. The cheetah's position gives the same displacement at the catch time, which is X sub C equals 1 half A sub C T squared. Equals 1 half times 4.0 meters per second squared times the quantity 5.0 seconds squared equals 50 meters. The conclusion. The cheetah catches the gazelle after 5.0 seconds. Both animals have traveled 50 meters from the starting point when the catch occurs.
